chunks: They exchanged the fortified palaces and the spread-out carpets,
the rocks and the leaning stones, and the flat, hollowed-out graves,
whose courtyards are built upon ruins, and whose construction was raised with soil,
so their location is contiguous, but their inhabitants are like strangers,
among the people of their neighborhood yet feeling lonely, and those free from work yet engaged (in activity),
they do not feel attachment to their homelands, nor do they maintain contact like neighbors,
despite what is between them of nearness of neighborhood and proximity of abodes,
and how can there be mutual visiting among them when decay has ground them with its millstone, and stones and earth have eaten them?
ai.seo_question: What is the contrast between worldly palaces and graves in Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (AS) employs vivid imagery of architectural decay to illustrate the *fana* (transience) of worldly status, contrasting the 'built-up' palaces of the living with the 'eroded' graves of the dead. This passage serves as a *dhikr* (remembrance) of death, urging believers to detach from material vanity and recognize the spiritual isolation that persists even amidst physical proximity. It underscores the Shia concept of *zuhd* (asceticism) not as mere poverty, but as an awareness of the inevitable return to the earth.
